newsitem.title: UK: UK producer prices show inflation still dormant.
newsitem.headline: UK producer prices show inflation still dormant.

text.p: British producer prices showed few signs of pipeline inflationary pressure in September even though official figures indicated headline factory gate prices jumped 0.4 percent on the month.
Analysts had forecast only a 0.1 percent rise but said much of the increase was due to soaring oil prices.
With core output prices climbing at their slowest rate in nearly 30 years, Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke will be in no hurry to raise interest rates, they said.
"They confirm developments further back along the inflation pipeline remain entirely favourable and should soon feed through to retail prices," said Jonathan Loynes at HSBC Markets.
Output prices leaving the factory gate rose 0.4 percent in September and 2.2 percent year-on-year, data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) showed.
Input prices, representing the cost to firms of raw materials and fuel prices, rose a seasonally adjusted 0.5 percent but were still 2.9 percent lower than a year ago.
Loynes said the rise in headline output prices was a little disappointing but attributed it largely to producers passing on higher oil prices.
Crude oil prices paid by UK industry rose by 7.0 percent in September and were 31.8 percent up year-on-year. The ONS said tensions in Iraq were largely responsible.

The United Nations suspended a deal whereby Iraq could sell oil in return for food and medicine after Iraqi President Saddam Hussein sent troops to intervene in fighting between Kurdish groups in the north of the country.

Once oil prices were taken out of the UK inflation equation, the data showed core output prices -- excluding food, drink, tobacco and petrol -- were up just 0.9 percent year-on-year, the lowest rate of increase since September 1967.
"The key core rate...suggests that underlying pressures are very subdued," said Jeremy Hawkins, economist at BankAmerica.

Analysts said Chancellor Clarke could use the figures as partial justification for leaving UK interest rates on hold and ignoring Bank of England Governor Eddie George's preference for base rates to be pushed up to 6.00 percent from 5.75.

"These data will be interpreted by the Chancellor and his advisers as evidence that there are few immediate inflation pressures to be worried about," said Warwick Lightfoot, economist at the Royal Bank of Scotland.
UK Treasury minister Angela Knight said the PPI numbers were an "excellent base" for falls in inflation in the high street.
But Kevin Gardiner, UK economist at Morgan Stanley, said to look at producer prices for signs of inflation was to look at the wrong end of the equation.
"PPI is a lagging indicator from the laggard part of the economy," he said. "We know retailers are upbeat, exports are reviving and that survey evidence is more bullish than the official figures."
He said inflationary pressure would come further up the chain, from retailers taking advantage of spiralling consumer spending to rebuild long-squeezed margins.
Gardiner said the next move for interest rates would probably be upwards. He forecast a 50 basis point increase, but not until February.
Alex Garrard, UK economist at UBSA, agreed consumer demand was taking off but said his research suggested retailers were still finding it difficult to make higher prices stick.

"As a result, it should not prove too difficult for the Chancellor to fend off the Governor's misgivings about the appropriate level of base rates at the next monetary meeting," he said. Clarke and George meet next on October 30.
